title: PGA Tour CEO calls Good Good’s initial response to controversial ad ‘concerning’
content:
ATLANTA — The PGA Tour made it clear Tuesday that it’s disappointed in Good Good Golf’s initial response to the public backlash over a controversial advertisement recently shared on the digital media and apparel brand’s social media channels.

When he was asked directly during a news conference ahead of this week’s Tour Championship whether Good Good took enough accountability, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp said: “I think, initially, no. I think what we saw was concerning (and) is clearly not aligned with PGA Tour values. We take it very seriously. I think their initial response was disappointing. It was a bit defensive and late.

“But I think the responses are getting better. I think we’ve seen some things this morning — we’ve had some conversations with them — so we’ll continue to monitor and work with them going forward. But, no, we were disappointed with what we saw.”

In the ad, which has been deleted, a female employee, Alexis Miestowski, reaches for a Good Good-branded Callaway driver in a bag. Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark charges at her from the background and pushes into her back with his forearm. She falls to the ground, he stands over her, and as she looks up at him, he says menacingly, “Do not touch my new driver.”

Good Good apologized Saturday amid significant online backlash for its depiction of casual violence toward women. “We posted a video to our channels that ultimately depicted actions that are not aligned with our values as a brand,” the statement read, in part.

Good Good, which has grown from a YouTube channel into an independent company that raised $45 million in 2025, is the name sponsor of a new PGA Tour event this fall — the Good Good Championship — which is scheduled for Nov. 12-15 at Omni Barton Creek in Austin, Texas. Rolapp was noncommittal about whether this controversy would affect that tournament.

“It’s a bit of a fluid situation,” Rolapp said. “We were disappointed at first. It sounds like in the last 24 hours they’ve made some progress. We’ll continue to monitor the situation and see how it develops.”

Callaway released a second apology early Tuesday morning, this one from CEO Chip Brewer, admitting it did view and approve the ad before it was posted.

“That approval should never have happened. Mistakes were made, and we are taking the matter very seriously,” Brewer’s statement read. “As we deal with the consequences of our mistake and complete our investigations, I want to make it clear that we sincerely apologize for the video. The content was inappropriate and does not reflect our values. To be clear: We are unequivocally against discrimination, domestic violence, or threatening behavior of any kind.”
